lead: A power BJT, a power MOSFET and an IGBT are three-terminal controlled switches. Each has a control terminal that decides whether the main path conducts. The BJT needs base current, the MOSFET needs gate voltage, and the IGBT needs gate voltage but conducts like a BJT. They exist because no single device is best at every voltage and current. You meet them in switch-mode power supplies, inverters, motor drives and electric-vehicle chargers. Choosing between them is mostly a question of conduction loss at your operating current.
prereq: You need: the diode static curve in Chapter 1.1, and the basic BJT and MOSFET from an earlier electronics course.

blocks.text: A power BJT is an NPN transistor built vertically: a heavily doped n+ emitter, a thin p base, a lightly doped n− drift region, and an n+ collector substrate. The drift region blocks voltage when the device is off. The base current controls the collector current. In the active region the collector current is set by the base current and the current gain.

blocks.where: I_C is the collector current in amperes, I_B is the base current in amperes, and β is the common-emitter current gain, dimensionless. Power BJTs have small β, often 5 to 20.

blocks.text: As a switch the BJT is either cut-off or in saturation. In cut-off the base is open and no current flows. In hard saturation both junctions are forward biased and the collector-emitter voltage falls to V_CE(sat), typically 1 V to 2 V. Before hard saturation the drift region is only partly filled with carriers; this quasi-saturation state has a higher V_CE and extra loss. A BJT needs continuous base current while on, so the driver burns power.

The weak point is the safe operating area. The base-emitter voltage falls as temperature rises, so a hotter spot in the die takes more current. That local current crowding can create a hot spot and secondary breakdown, which destroys the device even inside the rated power. Datasheets give a forward-bias SOA and a switching SOA. Keep the load line inside them.

A power MOSFET is a vertical structure with an n+ source, a p body, an n− drift region and an n+ drain. A thin oxide isolates the gate. Gate voltage, not gate current, controls the drain current: the gate charges a capacitance. Once charged, the gate draws almost no steady current.

blocks.where: P_cond is conduction loss in watts, I_D is drain current in amperes, and R_DS(on) is the on-state resistance in ohms at a stated gate voltage.

blocks.text: The on state is resistive. R_DS(on) has a positive temperature coefficient, so a hotter part of the die carries less current. This makes paralleling easy and removes secondary breakdown. The price is that conduction loss rises as I², so at high current the resistance hurts.

Every power MOSFET contains a body diode from the p body to the n drift region, antiparallel to the channel. In a bridge it conducts during dead time. It is a slow diode, so check its reverse recovery before relying on it.

Dynamic behaviour is set by gate charge Q_g and the Miller plateau. When the gate voltage reaches the threshold, the drain voltage starts to fall and the gate-drain capacitance holds the gate voltage almost flat. The driver must push charge through this plateau before the device is fully on. A larger plateau means slower switching and more switching loss.

An IGBT, insulated-gate bipolar transistor, combines a MOS gate with a bipolar output. The gate sits over a p body as in a MOSFET. A p+ layer is added at the collector, so the drift region fills with carriers: conductivity modulation. The output behaves like a BJT, with a collector-emitter saturation voltage V_CE(sat).

The common equivalent circuit is a MOSFET driving the base of a PNP transistor. Gate voltage turns the MOSFET on, which supplies base current to the PNP, and the main current flows from collector to emitter. The gate still needs only a short charge pulse.

Turn-off has a tail current. Stored charge in the drift region must be removed, so the collector current falls slowly at the end. This tail adds turn-off loss and limits the switching frequency. Many IGBTs block little or no reverse voltage; the datasheet may show a small reverse rating, and an external diode handles reverse current. Some modules include a freewheeling diode.

Selection follows the loss curves. MOSFET loss is I²R, a curve through zero. IGBT loss is V_CE(sat) × I plus a small resistive part, a line with an offset. At low current the MOSFET wins; at high current the IGBT wins. The crossover is where I² R_DS(on) = V_CE(sat) I, so I_cross = V_CE(sat) / R_DS(on).

figure.caption: The gate voltage drives a MOSFET section; that section supplies base current to a bipolar section, so the collector-emitter path carries the load current. Notice that the control input is a MOS gate, but the output is bipolar.

spec.title: IGBT equivalent
spec.aria: A gate voltage controls a MOSFET whose output drives the base of a bipolar transistor between collector and emitter.

examples.question: A power MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 0.1 Ω. An IGBT in the same circuit has V_CE(sat) = 2 V. Both carry a current I. (a) Find the conduction loss of each at 5 A and at 50 A. (b) Find the crossover current where the losses are equal. (c) State which device is better at each current.
steps: MOSFET conduction loss: P_M = I² R_DS(on). At 5 A, P_M = 5² × 0.1 = 25 × 0.1 = 2.5 W.
IGBT conduction loss: P_I = V_CE(sat) × I. At 5 A, P_I = 2 × 5 = 10 W. The MOSFET is better at 5 A.
At 50 A, P_I = 2 × 50 = 100 W. The IGBT is better at 50 A.
Set the losses equal: I² R_DS(on) = V_CE(sat) I. Cancel one I: I = V_CE(sat) / R_DS(on) = 2 / 0.1 = 20 A.
examples.answer: At 5 A the MOSFET dissipates 2.5 W against 10 W for the IGBT; at 50 A the MOSFET dissipates 250 W against 100 W; the crossover is 20 A, so the MOSFET is better below 20 A and the IGBT above.
examples.check:
R = 0.1
V = 2.0
for I in (5, 50):
    print(round(I*I*R, 6))
    print(round(V*I, 6))
print(round(V/R, 6))

traps: MOSFET conduction loss rises as I², not linearly. At 5 A a 0.1 Ω device loses 2.5 W, but at 50 A it loses 250 W. Do not use one loss figure for all currents.
The IGBT has a voltage offset V_CE(sat); it does not become a short circuit at low current. Its loss is roughly V_CE(sat) × I, not I²R.
Do not ignore the MOSFET body diode. In a half bridge it carries freewheeling current during dead time and its reverse recovery can cause voltage spikes.
Do not ignore the IGBT tail current when estimating turn-off loss; it adds a slow current fall that overlaps with rising voltage.
Quasi-saturation is not hard saturation. In quasi-saturation V_CE is higher, so the BJT dissipates more than the datasheet V_CE(sat) value suggests.

quiz.q: Name the control terminal and the controlled path of a power MOSFET.
quiz.a: The gate controls the drain-source current. The gate is voltage driven.

quiz.q: Why does a power MOSFET parallel well but a BJT does not?
quiz.a: MOSFET R_DS(on) rises with temperature, so a hot part takes less current. BJT V_BE falls with temperature, so a hot part takes more current and can suffer secondary breakdown.

quiz.q: A MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 0.05 Ω and carries 20 A. Find its conduction loss.
An IGBT has V_CE(sat) = 1.8 V at 30 A. Find its conduction loss.
What is the Miller plateau in a MOSFET turn-on?
quiz.a: It is the flat part of the gate-voltage waveform while the gate-drain capacitance charges and the drain voltage falls. The driver must supply charge through this plateau before the device is fully on.

quiz.q: Why does an IGBT show a tail current at turn-off?
quiz.a: The conductivity-modulated drift region stores charge. At turn-off that charge must be removed, so the collector current decays slowly at the end instead of stopping abruptly.

quiz.q: A circuit carries 8 A. A MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 0.2 Ω and an IGBT has V_CE(sat) = 2 V. Which has lower conduction loss and by how much?
quiz.a: MOSFET loss = 8² × 0.2 = 12.8 W. IGBT loss = 2 × 8 = 16 W. The MOSFET is lower by 16 − 12.8 = 3.2 W. The crossover current is 2 / 0.2 = 10 A, so at 8 A the MOSFET is the correct choice.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern IGBTs use trench gates and field-stop layers to trade off V_CE(sat) and switching speed. Reverse-conducting IGBTs integrate a diode on the same chip. At 1.2 kV and above, SiC MOSFETs are replacing IGBTs in electric vehicles and solar inverters. Search for “IGBT field stop”, “RC-IGBT” and “double pulse test” to see how these devices are characterised.
